entities.summary:
The Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem is a Constantinian-origin basilica traditionally marking the birthplace of Jesus, among the oldest continuously used Christian churches. Rebuilt under Justinian and contested by successive empires, it became a shared shrine of Greek Orthodox, Armenian, and Catholic custodianship.

Pilgrimage economies, crusader renovations, and Ottoman status-quo arrangements made the church a barometer of Christian holy-site politics. UNESCO listing and modern Palestinian–Israeli conflict further entangled its stones with diplomacy and tourism.

As architecture and sacred geography, the Nativity church concentrates two millennia of Christian memory in one contested Bethlehem compound.
